1.blurb: The Xiongnu were the original steppe political template that every later Inner Asian empire — Xianbei, Rouran, Türk, Mongol — inherited and refined. The decimal military organization, the dual eastern-western wing structure, the annual tribal assembly, the chanyu's claim to be the steppe's Son of Heaven equivalent of the Chinese emperor: every one of these elements that the Türks took for granted in 552 had been worked out by Modu Chanyu eight centuries earlier in the same Mongolian heartland.

The Avars who terrorized the Byzantine Empire under Justinian's successors may have been the same Rouran refugees who fled west after the Türk founding in 552 — though the identification is debated. If it holds, the Türk founding had a downstream consequence in central Europe within a single decade: the Rouran refugees built another steppe empire on the Hungarian plain that lasted until Charlemagne destroyed it in 796, and the Byzantine eastern frontier was destabilized for two centuries by what was, in effect, Türk collateral damage.

The Türk founding in 552 is almost exactly contemporary with Justinian's high-water mark in Byzantium — Hagia Sophia consecrated 537, the Pandects of Roman law completed 533, the reconquest of Italy and North Africa in progress. Justinian's general Belisarius was fighting the Ostrogoths in Italy in the same years that Bumin was destroying the Rouran in Mongolia, and within twenty years Türk and Byzantine envoys would be walking each other's courts in person via Maniakh's embassy.

The wolf-suckled twin founders are not unique to the Türks — Rome told the same of Romulus and Remus eight centuries earlier. The motif independently gave both peoples a usable myth of fierce, survivor bloodlines fit to found an empire.
Sasanian Persia under Khusrau I was at its height, and would be the Türks' ally-then-enemy within a few years — the steppe and the Iranian superpower entangled from the start.
Northern China was split between the Northern Zhou and Northern Qi — soon to be reunified by the Sui, the dynasty the Türks would spend a century manipulating.
On the Indian subcontinent the Gupta Empire was in its final decline as the Türk Khaganate rose — the classical order giving way across Eurasia at once.
In Mesoamerica the Maya were at their classical peak, simultaneous with everything in Eurasia and entirely unconnected to it.
Meanwhile in the Xiongnu & Huns story: the steppe superpower whose political template every later nomadic empire — including the Türks — inherited and refined.
Meanwhile in the Mongol Empire: the conqueror who, six centuries later, would claim the same khagan title the Türks helped make the universal Inner Asian imperial style.
Meanwhile in the Mongol Empire: the heirs who eventually pushed the steppe political system the Türks scaled up to its absolute limit.
Meanwhile in the Scythians' world: the earlier mounted nomads of the western steppe, the first of this app's grassland empires.
Meanwhile in the Byzantine Empire: the Roman successor state in Constantinople with whom Istemi's western Türks would open direct diplomatic contact.
Meanwhile in the Persian Empire: the Sasanian dynasty under Khusrau I, at its height — first the Türks' ally against the Hephthalites, then their enemy.
Meanwhile in the Byzantine Empire: Justinian's great domed cathedral in Constantinople, built in the same years Bumin was destroying the Rouran.
Meanwhile in the Goths' story: the Gothic kingdom in Italy that Justinian's general Belisarius was fighting as the Türk Khaganate was founded.
Meanwhile in China: the dynasty that would soon reunify the divided north and south — and become the Türks' great southern neighbor.

2.blurb: Genghis Khan's capital at Karakorum was built almost on top of the Türk khaganate's seasonal court site in the Orkhon Valley — the same broad upland river basin that had served as the political center for every successful Mongolian steppe empire from the Xiongnu onward. The Mongols were deliberately invoking a tradition of legitimacy that ran back through the Türks to the Xiongnu, and the geographic continuity of the Mongolian capital across two thousand years is one of the most striking spatial facts in pre-modern history.

The China that Bumin and Muqan exploited in the 550s and 560s was the late stage of the Six Dynasties era — North China divided between Northern Zhou and Northern Qi, both ruled by Xianbei-descended dynasties with steppe cultural roots, both willing to pay enormous silk tribute to keep the Türks out of their territory. Six Dynasties China's structural fragmentation was a precondition for Türk imperial success: the unified Sui that emerged in 589 would immediately break the tribute relationship and put the Türks under sustained pressure.

The 200,000 bolts of silk per year that Muqan extracted from the divided Chinese north was the largest tribute payment China had made to the steppe since the Han dynasty's heqin treaties seven centuries earlier. The Türks were deliberately replicating the Xiongnu-Han relationship — silk for peace, with the steppe empire dictating terms — but at a higher scale and with the added sophistication of moving the silk westward through the Sogdian merchant network for resale in Persian and Byzantine markets.
By 575 the Türk Khaganate was the largest political unit in Eurasia — dwarfing a Byzantium straining under the financial overstretch Justinian's reconquests had caused.
Sasanian Persia under Khusrau I was at its peak just as the Türk realm reached its maximum extent — two giants sharing a volatile border.
In the Andes the Tiwanaku and Wari states were emerging — the Türks touched everything in Eurasia but never the Americas, where parallel empires rose unconnected.
The Gupta Empire had collapsed into successor states by the time the Türk realm peaked — India's classical age ending as the steppe's apex began.

Meanwhile at the other end of the Türk diplomatic chessboard sat Constantinople, capital of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire — the city the khaganate's embassies traveled to in pursuit of the silk trade.
Chang'an, the great walled capital on the Wei River, would soon become the cosmopolitan heart of Tang China — the eastern terminus of the embassies and caravans the Türks dispatched.
The overland trade artery the Türks now controlled had been pried open centuries earlier by Han Emperor Wu's push into the western regions.
Seven centuries later another steppe conqueror would plant his capital almost exactly where the Türks centered theirs — Genghis Khan, who built Karakorum on the Orkhon.
The Xiongnu were the earlier steppe confederation whose dual-wing kingship and decimal army the Türks inherited and pushed further.
The Persia the western Türk wing dealt with was the Sasanian Empire, then at its sixth-century height under Khusrau I.
Türk silk flowed west into the Sasanian Persian markets — the empire then enjoying its Sassanid golden age under Khusrau I.
The Sasanian Persians were one of the great settled powers the Türks treated as a diplomatic equal, then at their peak under Khusrau I.
Byzantium — the Eastern Roman Empire ruled from Constantinople — was the western anchor of the Türk diplomatic world.
Justinian's costly reconquest of the western Mediterranean had left Byzantium financially overstretched just as the Türks rose in the east.
The southern dynasties along the Yangtze were ruled by Han Chinese, the ethnic majority that took its name from the earlier Han Empire.

Meanwhile the people who would one day replace the Türks on the steppe — the Uyghurs — were still subject tribes; in 840 they would topple the Türks' successors and build their own capital on the same Orkhon.

3.blurb: The full payoff of the Türk-Sogdian symbiosis described here — a foreign merchant diaspora becoming the administrative and cultural backbone of a steppe empire — arrived one empire later, with the Uyghurs. The Uyghurs took the same Sogdian partnership, added Manichaean state religion, built the Sogdian-descended Old Uyghur script into a literate administration, and ran the most commercially sophisticated nomadic state the steppe ever produced.

The Sogdian merchant diaspora is the closest pre-modern analogue to the medieval Sephardic Jewish trading network and the early modern Armenian merchant network. All three operated as multi-city kinship networks that combined commercial expertise, language skills, and political neutrality to handle long-distance trade for patron empires that could not have built equivalent commercial apparatus from scratch. The Sogdians ran the Silk Road for the Türks; the Armenians of New Julfa would run it for the Safavids; the Sephardim would run Mediterranean and Atlantic trade in the early-modern period.

The Sogdian merchant network had a deep precedent: the Phoenicians ran a similar Mediterranean-wide commercial diaspora 1,200 years earlier — though never at the Constantinople-to-Chang'an scale of the Sogdians.

A millennium later the Armenian merchants of New Julfa under Safavid Persia would build a strikingly similar state-aligned commercial diaspora — the same structure the Sogdians pioneered for the Türks.

Meanwhile in the Mongol Empire: the steppe-warrior-plus-conquered-bureaucracy model the Türks pioneered with the Sogdians would be inherited, six centuries later, by Genghis Khan's heirs — who likewise ran a Eurasian empire on borrowed administrators.

Meanwhile in the Byzantine Empire: Constantinople's silk-hungry market was the prize the Sogdians and their Türk patrons were chasing — and the reason they would soon attempt the most audacious end-run in steppe diplomacy, going around Persia entirely.

Meanwhile in Tang China: the great cosmopolitan dynasty whose capital Chang'an hosted Sogdian merchant colonies and whose silk tribute, piling up in the Türk treasury, set this whole chapter's commerce in motion.

Meanwhile in India: the Gupta Empire and the successor kingdoms that followed it were the southern end of the Sogdian trade web, reached through the several Indian languages the merchants kept on hand.

Meanwhile in the Byzantine Empire: Constantinople, the imperial capital on the Bosphorus, anchored the western end of the Sogdian diaspora — a documented Sogdian merchant community lived there in the seventh century.

Meanwhile in Central Asia eight centuries later: Samarkand, a Sogdian city in the Türk era, would become the glittering capital of Timur's empire, the high-water mark of Transoxiana's long history as a seat of power.
Meanwhile in the Byzantine Empire: the Greek-speaking Roman state on the Bosphorus, the Mediterranean buyer the Türks turned to once the Sasanians blocked their silk from the Persian market.

Meanwhile in Safavid Persia a thousand years later: the Armenian merchants of New Julfa served the shah as a state-aligned commercial diaspora in almost exactly the role the Sogdians played for the Türks — the closest functional parallel in all of history.

Meanwhile in the earlier steppe: the Xiongnu confederation fought Han China chronically for grain, iron, and silk — a raid-and-extort relationship with none of the commercial sophistication the Türk-Sogdian partnership brought to the trade.

Meanwhile in Iran: the Sasanian Persian Empire ran its own royal silk monopoly, turned away Sogdian silk as competition, and poisoned the Türk envoys sent to Khusrau I in 568 — the provocation that pushed the embassy toward Constantinople.

Meanwhile in Iran: Sasanian Persia was the immovable obstacle on the silk routes' western end, unwilling to buy Sogdian silk and unwise to fight just yet — the diplomatic problem this chapter sets up.

Meanwhile in the wider Islamic world: after the Arab conquest of Transoxiana, the old Sogdian cities of Bukhara and Samarkand were reborn as celebrated centers of learning and culture during the Islamic Golden Age.

4.blurb: The Hephthalites had been the Sasanian Empire's nightmare for almost a century before the Türk alliance crushed them. They had killed Shah Peroz I in battle in 484, captured the Persian camp, and forced annual tribute payments that humiliated the Sasanian court for forty years. Khusrau I's willingness to ally with the Türks in 557 reflected both the strategic logic of crushing a common enemy and the depth of Sasanian humiliation that any avenue to revenge was worth pursuing — even an alliance with steppe nomads.

Justin II's reception of Maniakh in 568 and dispatch of Zemarchus to Istemi the following year was one of the most far-reaching Byzantine diplomatic initiatives of the entire post-Justinian period. The alliance against the Sasanians was militarily inconclusive but politically remarkable: a steppe nomadic empire and the Eastern Roman Empire as great-power equals, exchanging embassies across thousands of miles, with Sogdian merchants providing the language skills and commercial infrastructure that made trans-Eurasian diplomacy possible.

Muhammad was born in Mecca in 570, two years after Maniakh's embassy reached Constantinople. The world that Muhammad would transform with the Islamic conquests starting in the 630s was the same world the Türks had just stitched together diplomatically: a Sasanian Persian Empire, a Byzantine Roman Empire, a Türk khaganate, and the Sogdian merchant network connecting them all. Within a century the Arab armies would erase two of those four players (Sasanian) and slowly digest the third (Sogdiana) on their way to Transoxiana.
The Sui reunification of China (589) was a generation away — the dynasty whose successor, the Tang, would ultimately conquer the Türk Khaganate.
Meanwhile in Persia: the Sasanian Empire under Khusrau I, the dynasty's most successful king, who reformed the army and tax system and allied with the Türks to destroy the Hephthalites.
Meanwhile on the earlier steppe: the Xiongnu, the first great nomadic empire of Inner Asia, whose disputed link to the western Huns shadows the question of who the Hephthalites really were.
Meanwhile in the west: the Huns of Attila — the European nomads whose connection to the Xiongnu and the Hephthalites' 'White Hun' label remains debated.
Later in China: the Tang dynasty, which would inherit the Türk-steppe relationship and play the same alliance-and-conquest game against later nomadic empires.
Meanwhile, centuries later: the Mongols, who repeated the steppe-and-settled crushing pattern against Khwarezm — the cleanest sequel to the Türk-Sasanian destruction of the Hephthalites.
Meanwhile, centuries later: the Khwarazmian Empire, the Central Asian power the Mongols obliterated — the later echo of the joint settled-and-steppe campaigns the Türks pioneered.
Meanwhile at the other end of Eurasia: the Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire, the third great settled power the Türks worked into their diplomacy to outflank Sasanian Persia.
Meanwhile in Constantinople: the emperor Justinian I, whose nephew and successor Justin II received Maniakh's Türk embassy in 568 and accepted the alliance against Persia.

5.blurb: The Sui Dynasty's reunification of China in 589 ended four hundred years of post-Han fragmentation and was the precondition for the disasters that befell the Türks across the next thirty years. A divided China had been the Türks' greatest geopolitical asset: Northern Zhou and Northern Qi competed to pay silk tribute, neither could mount a unified response, and Türk diplomatic-military leverage was overwhelming. Once the Sui consolidated both halves under one government, the leverage flipped, and the Türks moved from extracting tribute to fighting for survival.

Shibi's siege of the Sui Emperor at Yanmen Pass in 615 was a deliberate Türk replay of the Xiongnu humiliation of Han Gaozu at Baideng eight centuries earlier — the same trap structure (steppe cavalry surrounding the Chinese emperor and his vanguard), the same psychological objective (demonstrating that even a unified Chinese state could be humiliated), and the same political consequence (the Sui collapse, in echo of the Han near-collapse that produced the heqin treaties). Steppe leaders knew their history and quoted it back at China when convenient.

The Tang Dynasty founded in 618 with humiliating Türk help would become the dominant Eurasian power of the seventh and eighth centuries — the largest Chinese empire by territorial extent for the next thousand years, the most cosmopolitan capital city in the world at Chang'an, the patron of the An Shi mid-Tang cultural peak. Every Tang military and cultural success against the Türks across the next century was, in part, a deliberate effort to expunge the founding debt to Shibi's khaganate that nobody at court wanted to remember.

5.matchText: Muhammad's flight from Mecca to Medina
5.blurb: The Tang conquest of the Türks (630) is contemporary with the Hijra (622) and the early Islamic conquests — the Sasanian and Türk empires falling within a decade of each other to new powers rising east and west.
The Arab destruction of Sasanian Persia and the Tang destruction of the Türk Empire happened in the same span — two great pre-modern empires toppling within ten years.
Meanwhile in the earlier steppe: the Xiongnu were the first great nomadic empire, and their lateral succession habits and tribute extraction set the template the Türks inherited.
Meanwhile in Tang China: Chang'an, the dynasty's capital, grew into the cosmopolitan heart of the empire where surrendered Türk leaders and steppe envoys filled the court.

6.blurb: The Tang Protectorate System over the Türks was one component of a broader Tang frontier policy that also encompassed the Korean Peninsula (the Tang-Goguryeo wars of 645-668), Vietnam (the Annan Protectorate in modern northern Vietnam), and the Tarim Basin (Anxi). Taken together, these protectorates made the Tang Empire the largest Chinese empire by territory until the Qing — and the most administratively sophisticated frontier governance system any pre-modern Chinese dynasty ever attempted.

The Tibetan Empire's emergence as a major military power in the seventh century was one of the structural changes that eroded Tang grip on Central Asia. Tang military resources were committed to the Tibetan front from the 660s onward, weakening the empire's capacity to respond to renewed Türk activity in the north. The eighth-century three-way contest among Tang, Tibet, and the surviving Türk-derived peoples of the Tarim continued until the An Lushan Rebellion withdrew Tang forces from the western frontier permanently.

Empress Wu Zetian's rise to power in the late seventh century — culminating in her proclamation of the Zhou Dynasty in 690, the only time a Chinese woman has ruled in her own name — destabilized the Tang court enough to make sustained frontier policy impossible. Kutlugh's revolt in 682 was made possible by exactly this internal Tang turmoil, and the long-term decline of the Tang protectorate over the steppe began with Wu Zetian's elimination of the Tang princes who might have managed the frontier more effectively.
Meanwhile in China: the Tang dynasty, the cosmopolitan empire that conquered the Türks in 630 and ran the steppe through its protectorate system for fifty years.
Meanwhile in China: the Yellow River, the great northern artery whose Ordos bend the steppe powers and settled empires fought over for a thousand years.
Meanwhile on the steppe: the Xiongnu, the earlier nomadic confederation that contested the same Ordos frontier with Han China eight centuries before the Türks.
Meanwhile in China: Chang'an, the Tang capital and the most cosmopolitan city in the world, where the captured Türk khagan lived out his days as a court ornament.
Meanwhile on the steppe: the Uyghurs, one of the Tieli tribes folded under Tang authority who would later inherit the steppe from the Türks.
Meanwhile across Eurasia: the Silk Road, the caravan network the Tang protectorates and their Four Garrisons existed to keep open and safe.
Meanwhile in the Near East: the early Islamic conquests exploding out of Arabia, toppling the Sasanians and reshaping the western half of Eurasia in the same decades.
Meanwhile in Persia: the Sasanian Empire, the last pre-Islamic Persian dynasty, destroyed by the Arab armies in 651 as the Tang consolidated the eastern steppe.
Meanwhile in the Mediterranean: the emperor Heraclius and his heirs, fighting Byzantium's desperate survival war against the Arab onslaught.
Meanwhile in Mesoamerica: Teotihuacan, the great central-Mexican metropolis in decline just as the Tang protectorate flourished on the other side of the world.
Meanwhile in the Andes: the Wari state expanding toward its Middle Horizon peak in seventh-century Peru.
Meanwhile in the Andes: Tiwanaku, the highland power around Lake Titicaca, rising alongside Wari during the same Middle Horizon centuries.
Meanwhile in the Andes: the Middle Horizon, the era when Wari and Tiwanaku spread the first true Andean empires across the highlands.
Meanwhile in the Mediterranean: the Byzantine Empire, the eastern Roman state fighting for survival against the Arabs while the Tang ran the eastern steppe.
Meanwhile in the Americas: the Andes, where the Wari and Tiwanaku empires were peaking during the same seventh-century window.

7.blurb: The Han Empire's relationship with the Xiongnu — chronic warfare alternating with humiliating tribute, ending in the Xiongnu split and the Southern Xiongnu's absorption into the Chinese frontier system — provided the historical template that Bilge Kagan was reading and rejecting in his 732 inscription. Bilge knew Chinese history better than most Türk leaders and saw clearly what had happened to the Southern Xiongnu when they accepted Chinese silk and titles in exchange for political subordination: gradual loss of identity, eventual disappearance as a distinct people. The Orkhon Inscriptions are, in part, a deliberate attempt to keep the Türks from going the way of the Southern Xiongnu.

The Umayyad Caliphate's conquest of Sogdiana under Qutayba ibn Muslim in 705-715 effectively closed the Western Türk legacy in Central Asia, even though the Türks had not held that territory directly since the 660s. The Sogdian merchant cities that had been the economic spine of the Türk khaganate became Arab subjects, the Sogdian language went into long decline as Arabic and then New Persian replaced it, and the Sogdian commercial network was reorganized under Islamic auspices. Within two generations, Bukhara and Samarkand would be Muslim cities.

The Second Türk Khaganate's decades of conflict with the Tang Empire under Empress Wu Zetian, Emperor Zhongzong, and Emperor Xuanzong are one of the major frontier stories of the early-to-mid Tang period. The Tang court treated the Second Khaganate as a chronic management problem rather than an existential threat — a regional power to be contained rather than destroyed — and the policy was largely successful until Bilge's death in 734 brought instability back to the Türk side and made the 744 Uyghur takeover possible without major Tang involvement.

7.matchText: When you stayed in the Otuken forest and sent caravans, you had no troubles
7.blurb: The Uyghurs are the empirical case study for exactly the counsel Bilge delivered here. They ignored it: they built Ordu-Baliq (called Karabalghasun), the first true city ever raised by a steppe empire in Mongolia. The city Bilge warned against became the Uyghurs' defining achievement — and their fatal vulnerability. In 840 the Yenisei Kyrgyz destroyed it in a single campaign, and the Uyghur Khaganate was over by nightfall. Chapter 4 is that destruction.

7.matchText: Tonyukuk argued explicitly against Türk conversion to Buddhism
7.blurb: The Uyghurs broke with Tonyukuk's counsel here, but not in the way he feared. They did not convert to Buddhism — they converted to Manichaeism, the syncretic Persian religion Mani had founded in the third century. The structural consequences Tonyukuk warned against — a contemplative religion softening warrior culture, a foreign ideology reorganizing state power — arrived anyway, routed through a different scripture. Chapter 3 is the Manichaean conversion and what it actually produced.

Meanwhile in Tang China: Wu Zetian seized the regency and then the throne itself, becoming the only woman to rule China in her own name — the court chaos of her takeover is exactly what let Kutlugh's revolt succeed.
Meanwhile in China: the early Tang built the most powerful and cosmopolitan empire of the age, the settled colossus on the Türks' southern border that both fed and threatened the steppe.
Meanwhile on the steppe: the Uyghurs, a Türk subject people, would overthrow the Second Khaganate in 744 and inherit its place as masters of the Mongolian grasslands.
Meanwhile (centuries later): the Mongols would rise on the same steppe and, unlike the Türks, embrace Buddhism — exactly the path Tonyukuk had warned against.
Meanwhile in China: Chang'an was the Tang capital and the largest city on Earth, where Kapaghan's victims and severed enemies alike ended up — a war trophy displayed at the imperial court.
Meanwhile across Eurasia: the Silk Road ran smoothly under joint Tang and Türk protection, with Sogdian merchants paying the khaganate handsome commissions for safe passage.

Meanwhile in northern Europe: the Germanic peoples carved their own runes into stone — angular letters that look like the Old Turkic script by coincidence, not contact (sharp tools on hard stone produce similar shapes).
Meanwhile (two centuries earlier): Attila led the Huns against Rome, but everything we know of him comes from his enemies — unlike Bilge, who speaks for himself in the Orkhon stones.

Meanwhile in the west: the Umayyad Caliphate was conquering Sogdiana, Spain, and pushing to the gates of France — the Second Khaganate's lifespan overlaps almost exactly with the great Arab conquests.

Meanwhile in Iberia: the Visigothic kingdom of Spain, the last Gothic state in the West, fell to the Umayyad invasion of 711 — the same wave of conquest that closed out the Western Türk legacy in Central Asia.
Meanwhile in the eastern Mediterranean: the Byzantine Empire, the surviving Roman state, was the great power the Western Türks had once allied with against Persia and was now fighting off the Arabs.
Meanwhile in the west: Constantinople, the Byzantine capital, survived the second great Arab siege of 717–718 under Leo III — the same years Bilge Kagan was consolidating the steppe.

Meanwhile in Britain: the patchwork of Anglo-Saxon kingdoms was producing its own literate culture, where the monk Bede was writing the history of the English Church the same year the Türk inscriptions were carved.

8.blurb: The An Lushan Rebellion of 755-763 was the single most consequential event in mid-Tang history — and it was led by a half-Sogdian, half-Türk general whose biography embodied the long aftermath of the Türk collapse. The rebellion's near-destruction of the Tang dynasty, the Uyghur cavalry intervention that rescued the dynasty, and the permanent Tang withdrawal from Central Asia that followed all flowed from the Türk-Sogdian-Tang frontier system that Tang Taizong had built and that broke definitively with An Lushan.

The Battle of Talas in 751 is the moment when the Islamicization of Central Asia became inevitable, and the Karluks' battlefield defection from the Tang to the Abbasid side was the decisive event. Within two centuries the Karluks themselves would be Muslim, the Sogdian oases would be Muslim, and the Türk-speaking peoples of Central Asia would have begun the long process of converting to the religion that the Seljuks and Ottomans would carry into the Middle East. The religious geography of the modern Islamic world traces back through Talas to one Türk-descended people's choice on one battlefield.

The Battle of Manzikert in 1071 is one of the most consequential defeats in Byzantine history — Sultan Alp Arslan's Seljuks captured Emperor Romanos IV, broke Byzantine control of central Anatolia, and opened the highlands to Türk-speaking nomadic settlement. Within a generation the cultural transformation of Anatolia from Greek-speaking Christianity to Türk-speaking Islam was underway, and the eventual Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453 was the long-delayed consequence of what Manzikert had set in motion three and a half centuries earlier.

The Ottoman dynasty founded around 1299 by Osman I traces its self-identification as Türk back through the Anatolian Seljuks to the Oghuz steppe confederations to the Western Türk subject peoples to the Ashina founding in 552. The Ottomans understood themselves as the latest carriers of an unbroken Türk political tradition, and Ottoman court culture preserved Türk-language poetry and political vocabulary even as the dynasty operated in a Persianate-Arabic-Turkish multilingual environment for six centuries.

When Genghis Khan declared himself khagan in 1206, he was deliberately invoking a tradition that ran back through the Khitan Liao Dynasty, the Uyghur Khaganate, and the Türk Khaganate to Bumin in 552. The Mongol Empire is in many ways a continuation of the Türk political template — same dual-wing organization, same decimal military system, same Tengri-based legitimating ideology, same khagan title — and even the Mongols' inherited Uyghur script descended from the Sogdian alphabet via the Türks' own administrative practice.

The post-Türk Turkic diaspora that produced the Karluks, Karakhanids, Khwarezmians, and Seljuks is one of the great population-and-language stories of early Islamic history. Every later Türk-speaking Muslim state — from the Ghaznavids to the Karakhanids to the Seljuks to the Mamluks to the Khwarezmians to the Ottomans — descended in some sense from the Western Türk-derived peoples who began their long Islamic conversion after the Karluk defection at Talas in 751.

8.blurb: The Uyghur Khaganate that replaced the Türks in 744 is the subject of its own narrative now. The full story — how they built the only Manichaean steppe state in history, how they became the Tang dynasty's indispensable creditor and military rescuer, how 840 ended everything — is told there from the start.
Meanwhile in China: the Tang dynasty, which the Uyghurs rescued from the An Lushan Rebellion in exchange for silk subsidies and parity of status.
Meanwhile in China: the Tang state, whose westward push into Central Asia collided with the Abbasids at the Battle of Talas in 751.
Meanwhile in China: Tang China, the great eastern power the steppe peoples alternately served, rescued, and raided.
Meanwhile in Iran: the deep Persian tradition whose language and culture saturated Central Asia before the Arab and Türk conquests.
Meanwhile in China: Chang'an, the Tang capital the Uyghur cavalry helped retake from An Lushan's rebels.
Meanwhile across Asia: Buddhism, the faith the displaced Uyghurs of the Tarim Basin gradually adopted in place of Manichaeism.
Meanwhile in the Islamic world: the Umayyad dynasty, overthrown by the Abbasids in 750 just before the Talas confrontation.
Meanwhile in Iran: Samarkand, one of the great Sogdian-Iranian oasis cities that began converting to Islam after Talas.
Meanwhile in China: the Silk Road, the trans-Eurasian trade network the Sogdians ran and the steppe empires taxed.
Meanwhile on the steppe: the Mongol Empire, in many ways a continuation of the Türk political template four centuries later.
Meanwhile on the steppe: the Mongols, Türk-adjacent conquerors who inherited the entire steppe political tradition from the Türks.
Meanwhile on the steppe: the Mongol invasions of the 1230s that swept away the last Türk-speaking confederations of the western steppe.
Meanwhile on the steppe: the Khitan Liao dynasty, a link in the chain of khagan-titled steppe states running from the Türks to Genghis Khan.
Meanwhile in the Mediterranean: the Byzantine Empire, the Christian power the western Türk peoples raided, allied with, and finally displaced from Anatolia.
Meanwhile in the Mediterranean: Byzantium, whose loss of Anatolia after Manzikert opened the region to Türk settlement.
Meanwhile in the Mediterranean: Constantinople, the Byzantine capital the Ottomans finally took in 1453.
Meanwhile in southeastern Europe: the Balkans, the European heartland of the Ottoman Empire, the last and longest-lasting post-Türk state.
Meanwhile in Iran: the Persian Gulf, a frontier of the multi-continental Ottoman realm at its height.
Meanwhile in the Islamic world: Baghdad, the Abbasid capital the Seljuks seized in 1055, taking the title of Sultan from the figurehead caliph.
Meanwhile on the steppe: the Xiongnu, the earlier nomadic confederation whose traditions the Türks inherited.
Meanwhile in the Mediterranean: the Phoenicians, another pivot-people who gave the world the alphabet and then vanished as a distinct nation.
